title: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Carbon, Its Strongest Model for Coding and Cyber Defense
excerpt: Carbon tops the Artificial Analysis index at 59 and leads key cybersecurity benchmarks, but access starts with a vetted group of cyber defenders, not the public.
body:
• Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, calling it its strongest model, two weeks after launching Gemini 4 Argon.
  • Carbon ranks No. 1 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 at 59, with 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, 54.8% on ExploitGym and 71.0% on CWE-bench for cybersecurity tasks.
  • Access is restricted at first: a subset of cyber defenders this week, then trusted partners through Google's Fairwind Program, before developers and consumers.
  • Introductory pricing matches Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input 95% off — but most developers cannot use Carbon yet.

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, describing it in its official announcement as its strongest model, with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. The launch comes two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, a pace Google attributed to its researchers and models working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster.

The benchmark claims

Carbon ranks No. 1 on the recently updated v5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59, according to Google and confirmed in coverage by 9to5Google. On cybersecurity, Google claimed a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro at 88.2% for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym at 54.8% for exploitation, and CWE-bench at 71.0% for patching. On internal benchmarks, the company said Carbon more than doubled Argon's success rate at generating secure code, and that its Chrome team saw Carbon perform more than ten times better than another lab's frontier model at generating high-quality patches.

https://x.com/Google/status/2115489522603466766

"On cybersecurity, Google claimed a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro at 88.2% for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym at 54.8% for exploitation, and CWE-bench at 71.0% for patching."

For general coding and web development, Google said Carbon jumped 89 Elo points to No. 4 at 1768 on WebDev Arena, with improvements across coding, agentic and scientific tasks, full-stack web development and multimodal understanding, building on user feedback after Argon.

Built for long-horizon work

Google positioned Carbon for sustained agentic workflows rather than single prompts. Internal teams, the company said, have seen Carbon run for days, persisting through dead ends to root-cause and patch subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. That long-horizon claim is the core of the pitch to engineering organizations: a model that can carry a multi-step task to completion instead of producing a single answer.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=A78IwMQSWc0

Safety and alignment claims

Google said Carbon builds on Argon's multi-layered safety stack, including prompt-injection resilience and chain-of-thought monitoring. It reported that high-severity misalignment alerts in live coding environments with its own teams fell by almost 80%, that successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 dropped to 0.0%, and that Carbon achieved a 0.0% attack success rate on the Gray Swan indirect prompt injection benchmark. The company also said Carbon cuts unsupported claims by roughly half compared with Argon, reduces overreach by 26% and under-service by 29%. These are Google's internal measurements, reported as the company stated them.

Who gets it, and when

Most readers cannot use Carbon today. Google said it is taking a deliberate approach to rollout and is engaged in the US government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, Carbon will be available to a subset of cyber defenders, then gradually to additional trusted partners through its Fairwind Program, before a broader release to developers, businesses and consumers. 9to5Google reported the same staged plan and noted introductory pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising afterward to $4 and $20.

What it means for developers in India and the diaspora

For Indian and diaspora engineering teams, the practical news is timing, not benchmarks: the strongest claimed gains are in exactly the work — secure code generation, vulnerability patching, long-running maintenance — that large IT services firms sell. But until Fairwind access widens and a public API date is set, Carbon is a capability to plan around rather than a tool to adopt. Watch for Google's developer release announcement, which will confirm final pricing and availability.
